You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

The roller wheel on my sliding closet door snapped. I've got two 608 skateboard bearings and an M8 bolt I could use. Could I 3D print a new wheel that spins on the bolt? The old one was about 50 mm across and about 16 mm wide.

The user wants a closet door roller wheel, 50mm across and 16mm wide, running on two 608 bearings with an M8 bolt. The hardware list has M8 screws up to 50mm long, and the bolt they mentioned is theirs to use, so I'll plan around the ISO 4762 screws with an ISO 4032 nut and an ISO 7089 washer. The main open question is the bearing outer diameter, which I still need to measure.

I'm still checking a few open questions: the bearing outer diameter needs re-measuring since the earlier reading didn't match the 22mm I assumed, I need to know whether the track has a V or U groove or is flat, and I want the gap between the bracket arms and the bolt length. I'll take those measurements together.

I'm settling the wheel profile: a 50 mm outer diameter and 16 mm width, with a flat tread and small chamfers on the edges, since I don't know the track shape and I'll note that. Two 7 mm bearings take up 14 mm of the 16 mm width, which leaves room for a central lip between them.

I'm working out the bearing pockets: 7 mm deep from each face leaves a 2 mm internal shoulder, and since the inner rings of the two bearings would sit 2 mm apart, I want a small 2 mm spacer between them so the clamping bolt doesn't load the bearings axially. I'll also size the bearing pocket at about 22.1 mm for a snug press fit in printed PLA, and plan a test coupon to check it.

I'm weighing whether to print three coupon pockets at 21.95, 22.1, and 22.25 mm to pick the best fit, keeping the pocket size as one parameter with offsets. For printing, the wheel lies flat with the pockets facing up from both sides. The 2 mm internal shoulder leaves a flat annular overhang about 3 mm wide, which is probably acceptable for PLA, though a chamfered underside would stop the lower bearing from seating properly.

I'm weighing the bolt length now: the wheel is 16 mm wide, and adding the bracket plates, washers and an M8 nut pushes the stack to roughly 30 mm, so an M8x35 ISO 4762 seems the safer choice, though I still don't know the bracket width.

I'm considering the washer size now: an OD of 16 mm could rest on the bearing shields, so I'd want a smaller washer or a recessed face to keep the load on the inner rings only.

I'm weighing whether to make the outer spacers thin rings of about 11.5 mm OD so they touch only the inner rings, but if the bracket gap is only 16 to 17 mm they may not fit at all, so I'll treat them as optional.

I'm settling the coupon: a 30 mm disc, 9 mm tall, with the same 7 mm pocket and 2 mm shoulder as the wheel, so it tests the real geometry. I'm also starting a parameter list with the bearing OD at 22 mm.

I'm working through the parameter list now: the bearing bore and the bearing's inner-ring diameter are datasheet values, the wheel dimensions come from the brief, and the spacer is sized at 2 mm to match the shoulder gap.
